collection.description: It looks so much like a villager that it's unsettling.

ask.text:
(potter), the village potter, has found a new bank of clay up the river, red and very smooth. (subject.He/She) has been making little figures of people from it, and they are so lifelike that everyone wants one. Today (subject.he/she) has made one of (subject), sitting on (subject.his/her) shelf to dry. It looks so much like (subject) that it's unsettling.
The trouble is, the old potters used to say that red river clay remembers what it was shaped into, and given enough heat, tries to become it. (potter) laughs about that. Should (subject) let the figure be fired in the kiln tonight, or ask (potter) to squash it back into a lump?

c1o1.text: In the morning, when (potter) opens the kiln, a full-sized person climbs out of it, dusting ash off (subject.his/her) shoulders. It is (subject), exactly: same face, same scar, same laugh. (potter) drops the pot (subject.he/she) is holding. The new (subject) catches it. The village names (subject.him/her) (made1), and (potter) never touches red clay again.

c1o2.text: Someone climbs out of the kiln in the morning who looks just like (subject), but who was made by (potter)'s hands, not (subject)'s life. It likes what (potter) likes, hates what (potter) hates, and calls itself (made1). (subject) and the newcomer get on surprisingly well, mainly by complaining about (potter) together.

c1.text: (potter) slides the little figure into the kiln with the evening's pots and banks up the fire. All night the kiln glows and ticks and sighs...

c2o1.text: The clay squirts out between (potter)'s fingers and drops onto the floor in {#made:one lump|two lumps}, which grow, and stand up, and become {#made:a copy|two copies} of (subject), exact in every way, looking very offended. "That hurt," {#made:it says|they say together}. The village names {#made:the newcomer (made1)|them (made1) and (made2)}, and (potter) takes the rest of the red clay back up the river.

c2o2.text: It squishes into a lump, the way clay does. (potter) rolls it into a ball and makes a bowl out of it instead. It is a perfectly ordinary bowl. Except that (subject) is sure, every time (subject.he/she) eats from it, that it has a faint look of (subject.him/her) about the rim.

c2.text: "Squash it," says (subject). (potter) sighs, picks up the figure and squeezes it in (subject.his/her) fist. The clay is warm. It squirms...
